sections.1.0:
Welcome to the Bitcoin Diploma. Over the next ten weeks you'll build up an understanding of money — what it actually is, why it works the way it does, and where Bitcoin fits into that story.

You'll notice ShalaKasi popping up throughout the course. ShalaKasi isn't a real person — it's your AI mentor, built right into this platform to guide you through the Diploma. Ask it anything, any time you're stuck. Nobody in this room gets left behind.

Before we touch Bitcoin at all, we need to answer a much older question: why does money exist in the first place? It's tempting to skip straight to Bitcoin — it's the exciting part, after all — but doing that would be like trying to understand why a car's engine matters without first understanding why humans wanted to travel faster than walking. Money is a tool humans built to solve a very old, very human problem, and until you understand that problem clearly, Bitcoin will just look like a strange kind of internet money instead of what it actually is: an attempt to solve that same old problem in a new way.

This course is structured deliberately. Chapters 1 through 5 are entirely about money — its history, its properties, and the ways it can go wrong. Only in Chapter 6 do we actually arrive at Bitcoin itself. That's not padding. Everything you learn about money in the first half becomes the lens you'll use to evaluate Bitcoin in the second half.
sections.1.1:
Meet ShalaKasi — that's me. I'm here to help you through this Diploma: explaining ideas a different way when something doesn't click, flagging useful resources, and keeping track of where you're strong and where you need another pass.

Let's start with something personal. Think about your own life here in Ekasi — the taxi you took this morning, the airtime you bought, the money your family sends between each other. All of that runs on an assumption most people never question: that money works.

Before we define it properly, answer honestly, in your own words: what do you actually use money for, day to day?

Here's a thought experiment worth sitting with before you answer: imagine waking up tomorrow and every rand note, every coin, and every number in every bank account in the country simply vanished overnight — but everything else stayed exactly the same. The taxis still run, the shops still have stock, people still have the same skills and the same needs. What would happen in the first hour? The first day? The first week?

Most people's instinct is that chaos would follow almost immediately — and that instinct is worth trusting. It tells you something important: money isn't just a convenience sitting on top of a working economy. It's closer to the nervous system of that economy — the thing that lets millions of separate decisions by strangers who've never met coordinate with each other. A taxi driver doesn't need to know anything about the person who grew the maize that became their breakfast. Money is what makes that possible without either of them needing to know the other exists.
sections.1.2:
Now that you've thought about money on your own, let's open it up as a group.

Some questions worth sitting with: Why do our parents trade hours of their time for money instead of just being given what they need directly? Why does the same amount of money buy less than it used to? Why is the rand worth something different in Cape Town than the dollar is in New York?

There's no single right answer yet — the goal of this discussion is just to notice that money is stranger, and more designed, than it first appears.

A few more angles to bring into the discussion, if the conversation needs fuel: Why do some countries' currencies hold their value for decades while others lose most of their value within a few years? Why did older generations sometimes keep cash 'under the mattress' rather than in a bank, and were they wrong to? Why does a R200 note cost almost nothing to produce, yet people will work a full day to earn one? Sit with the fact that none of these are trick questions — they're the actual questions this Diploma is going to answer, one chapter at a time. By Chapter 10, you should be able to answer every one of them with real confidence, not just a guess.
sections.2.0:
In Chapter 1 we asked why money is necessary. Now we go one level deeper: what actually is money?

It turns out humans have used wildly different objects as money throughout history — cattle, salt, shells, cigarettes in a prison economy, gold, paper notes, and now numbers in a banking app. What single idea connects all of these?

Here's a useful way to test your own intuition before reading further: picture three very different objects — a cow, a gold coin, and the number displayed in your banking app. On the surface they have almost nothing physically in common. One is alive, one is a lump of dense yellow metal, and one is just electricity representing information on a server somewhere. Yet all three have, at different points in history and in different places, done the exact same job for the people using them. That's the puzzle this chapter untangles: money isn't defined by what it's made of. It's defined by the job it does and the agreement people have about it.
sections.2.1:
People often assume money just means the coins and notes in their pocket, or the number on a banking app screen. But that's only what money looks like today — not what makes it work.

Throughout history, wildly different things have served as money: cattle, salt, shells, gold, even cigarettes inside a prison economy. What they had in common wasn't their shape or material. It was a shared, trusted agreement that this object could reliably store and transfer value between people.

Money isn't a thing — it's an agreement that a thing represents value. That distinction matters, because it means money is a technology: a tool humans built to solve a coordination problem. Like any tool, some versions of it work better than others, depending on which qualities they hold onto over time.

The prison-cigarette example is worth pausing on, because it strips money down to its rawest form. Prisoners don't have banks, governments, or printed currency — yet cigarette-based economies have been documented forming spontaneously and consistently across very different prison systems in different countries. Why cigarettes specifically, rather than, say, socks or soap? Because cigarettes happened to have several useful properties at once inside that environment: they came in identical, easily countable units; they were durable enough to hold and trade without spoiling quickly; they were scarce enough that nobody could simply manufacture more; and — critically — even non-smokers accepted them, because everyone knew someone else would too. That last point is the real seed of what money is: an object becomes money not because of what it's physically capable of, but because enough people expect everyone else to also accept it. Once that expectation is widely shared, the object becomes remarkably powerful, almost regardless of what it's made of.
sections.2.2:
Beyond just storing value, money does three specific jobs in an economy. It's a medium of exchange — something both sides of a trade accept, solving the double-coincidence problem covered back in Chapter 1. It's a unit of account — a common way to price and compare wildly different things (how many chickens equal a bicycle? Price both in the same currency and the comparison becomes trivial). And it's a store of value — a way to hold wealth from today into the future without it rotting, being stolen, or evaporating.

A form of money that does all three jobs well tends to win out over ones that only manage one or two.

It helps to see what happens when something is good at only one or two of these jobs, not all three. Consider frequent-flyer miles: they work reasonably well as a unit of account within a narrow context (you can compare the 'price' of different flights in miles) and can act as a limited medium of exchange between a customer and one airline. But almost nobody treats them as a genuine store of value — airlines can devalue them overnight by changing the exchange rate, and they're worthless outside that one company's ecosystem. Or consider a bag of rice: it's an excellent store of value in the very short term and can be traded directly, but it's a poor unit of account (nobody prices a house 'in bags of rice') and it eventually spoils, failing as a long-term store of value. Real, widely-used money is unusual precisely because it does a passable job at all three simultaneously, across an entire society, for a long stretch of time. That combination is harder to achieve than it first sounds — which is exactly why the next few sections examine the specific properties that make it possible.
sections.2.3:
If money is a tool, what makes one version of that tool better than another? Economists generally point to a handful of properties:

— Durability: it shouldn't rot, rust, or fall apart.
— Portability: you should be able to carry it and move it easily.
— Divisibility: it should split into smaller units for small trades.
— Scarcity: it can't be endlessly created, or it loses value.
— Fungibility: one unit should be interchangeable with another.
— Recognizability and verifiability: people need to trust it's genuine.

Cattle score badly on portability and divisibility — try splitting a cow into bus fare. Gold solved several of these better, which is exactly why it became the dominant form of money for thousands of years, right up until the systems we'll unpack in the next few chapters replaced it with paper.

It's worth walking through cattle against every single property, because seeing exactly where a familiar example fails makes the abstract list much more concrete. Cattle are reasonably durable (a healthy cow lasts years) and are somewhat scarce (you can't conjure a cow from nothing). But they fail badly on portability — try herding livestock across a mountain range to trade in the next village — and they fail completely on divisibility, since a cow can't be split into smaller units without destroying its value entirely. They're also poor on fungibility: one cow is never quite identical to another in health, age, or temperament, which makes trades harder to agree on than they should be. Gold improves on nearly every one of these at once — it doesn't rot, it can be melted into standard-sized units, it's identical atom-for-atom regardless of which mine it came from, and it's rare enough that nobody can simply will more of it into existence. Its one real weakness, portability at scale (a large amount of gold is genuinely heavy and hard to move or verify quickly), is precisely the weakness that later chapters show fiat paper — and eventually Bitcoin — each try to solve in very different ways.
sections.2.4:
Money can be sorted into a few broad categories. Commodity money has value from the material itself — gold, silver, salt — usable even if nobody agreed to treat it as money. Representative money is a claim on a commodity held elsewhere, like an early banknote redeemable for gold. Fiat money has value purely by government decree and public trust, backed by nothing physical — covered in full in Chapter 4. And digital money exists only as entries in a database or ledger, which describes most money in circulation today, Bitcoin included.

Noticing which category something falls into is often the fastest way to spot its actual weaknesses.

A useful habit to build right now, early in the Diploma, is to run this categorization on any form of money you encounter for the rest of the course — including, eventually, Bitcoin itself in Chapter 6. Ask: does this thing have value independent of anyone's agreement to accept it (commodity money), is it a paper or digital claim on something else that's actually scarce (representative money), does it rely purely on collective trust and legal enforcement with nothing physical behind it (fiat money), or does it exist only as entries in some ledger somewhere (digital money)? Notice that these categories aren't mutually exclusive over time — gold started as pure commodity money, then much of it became representative money once banks issued gold-backed paper notes, and eventually that same paper became pure fiat money once the gold backing was removed. That transition — representative money quietly becoming fiat money — is one of the most consequential shifts in monetary history, and it's exactly what Chapters 3 and 4 trace in detail.
sections.2.5:
Money isn't just a mechanical tool — it shapes behavior in predictable psychological ways. Scarcity is one clear example: people tend to value what's limited more than what's abundant, which is part of why gold historically held value and why Bitcoin's fixed 21 million supply matters so much to the people who use it.

Time preference is another: how much someone values a reward now versus a larger reward later. Money that reliably holds its value over time tends to encourage saving and long-term thinking — sound money rewards patience. Money that loses value quickly does the opposite, pushing people toward spending immediately rather than saving, since waiting only costs them purchasing power.

Activity: work through the Time Preference activity with your group — trading a smaller reward now against a larger one later reveals a lot about how differently people are wired for this, and why the money system itself shapes those instincts over time.

Time preference is worth understanding as something that isn't fixed — it responds to the environment a person is in, including the monetary environment. Consider two people, identical in every way, placed into two different economies. In the first economy, prices are stable or even falling slightly year over year, so R100 saved today will comfortably buy at least as much in five years. In the second economy, prices rise 20% every year, so that same R100 will buy noticeably less in just twelve months. Even without changing anything about either person's character, you'd expect very different saving behavior between them — not because one person is more disciplined, but because the first economy rewards patience and the second actively punishes it. This is a genuinely important idea to hold onto going into Chapter 5, because it reframes something people often treat as a personal failing — 'people today just don't save enough' — as something that might instead be a predictable, rational response to the specific monetary system they're living inside.
